title: Training ML Models with Predictable Failures
abstract: Estimating how often an ML model will fail at deployment scale is central to pre-deployment safety assessment, but a feasible evaluation set is rarely large enough to observe the failures that matter. Jones et al. (2025) address this by extrapolating from the largest k failure scores in an evaluation set to predict deployment-scale failure rates. We give a finite-k decomposition of this estimator's forecast error and show that it has a built-in bias toward over-prediction in the typical case, which is the safety-favorable direction. This bias is offset when the evaluation set misses a rare high-failure mode that the deployment set contains, leaving the forecast to under-predict at deployment scale. We propose a fine-tuning objective, the forecastability loss, that addresses this failure mode. In two proof-of-concept experiments, a language-model password game and an RL gridworld, fine-tuning substantially reduces held-out forecast error while preserving primary-task capability and achieving safety similar to that of supervised baselines.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a genuine pre-deployment safety problem—forecasting rare failures at deployment scale—and proposes a concrete training objective that demonstrably reduces forecast error while preserving task performance, which could influence how teams approach safety evaluation pipelines.

novelty.justification: The key contribution—using the differentiable forecast error itself as a fine-tuning loss to shape failure tails—is a novel application of extreme value theory to training, distinct from prior work on tail-aware optimization or evaluation-aware training, though it builds incrementally on Jones et al.'s forecasting framework.

reproducibility.justification: The method is clearly described with mathematical detail and the paper includes algorithmic specifics (partition-invariant caching, improving-only mask), but no code, weights, or datasets are mentioned as public, requiring reimplementation effort for reproduction.

clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear motivation, rigorous mathematical exposition of the error decomposition, and concrete experimental instantiation; however, the dense theoretical sections and heavy notation may limit accessibility to practitioners unfamiliar with extreme value theory.

topical_fit.justification: Directly addresses a core concern for LLM builders—pre-deployment safety assessment and failure forecasting—and demonstrates the approach on both language models and RL, making it highly relevant to the editorial position on applied LLM systems.
